newsitem.title: USA: FUND VIEW - Flows for US funds seen strong in Feb.
newsitem.headline: FUND VIEW - Flows for US funds seen strong in Feb.

text.p: While not seen matching the lofty, often record-setting levels of January, cash flows into U.S. stock mutual funds were nonetheless expected to be robust this month, mutual fund firms said on Wednesday.
"The small investor's love affair with stock funds continues unabated," said Laurence Dwyer, a spokesman for New England Investment Cos LP.
The big sector winners so far in February have been index, growth, blue chip and international funds, the firms said.
Analysts cited the strong performance in U.S. stocks for the healthy January showing.

"The market has done very well and that's attracted money," said Charles Biderman, president of Mutual Fund Trim Tabs. The Investment Company Institute estimated earlier on Wednesday that net new cash flow into U.S. stock mutual funds was $24 billion in January. The total is up from $12.22 billion in December, but not as high as the record of $28.9 billion in January 1996.
Vanguard Group recorded total inflows of $4.9 billion in January, a record, with about $3.4 billion in equity funds.
"It appears that February is going to be on target to rival January, but it probably won't beat January," said Vanguard spokesman Brian Mattes.

The popular funds so far this month, said Mattes, have been index, large blue chip and growth and income. Mattes noted that tax-free bond funds were also showing strong trends, due in part to the upcoming U.S. tax season. In January, inflows into tax-free bond funds were five times the December rate.
Mattes traced the strong overall flows to a "very strong stock market right out of the of box in January...Investors tend to want to invest when the market is going up."
The Dow Industrials average was up nearly six percent in January and the S&P 500 index performed even better, rising 6.1 percent.
Charles Schwab Corp said net new cash flow into stock funds totalled about $430 million through February 11 versus $653 million in the same January period.
So far this month, the strongest sectors were domestic growth at $216 million and international growth at $137 million, spokesman Glen Mathison said.
New England experienced "a record month in January" and "it looks like another strong month in February," said Dwyer.

New England declined to provide data, saying only that inflows rose 35 percent in January versus December and jumped 40 percent compared with January 1995, Dwyer said. The biggest flows were in domestic growth and worldwide funds.
T. Rowe Price Associates Inc also set a cash flow record in January, although it also declined to provide details. The company recorded total inflows of $1.6 billion in January 1996.
Analysts do not expect flows to abate in the event of a correction in U.S. stocks.

"Even if we see market volatility, the underlying commitment to stock and fund investments is very strong and a price decline is not going to be enough to break that commitment," said Avi Nachmany, head of research at Strategic Insight, a fund research firm.
